I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a clear, cold sound at night, running over stones and through the meadow. I can also hear the rain when it comes, and the frogs in the marsh. The stream is where I go to drink, and I can find it by the sound even when the mist is thick.

I hear the stream by the meadow, and the brook that runs through the wood. At night, the water sings with the wind, and I can tell where it is by the sound. Sometimes I hear the frogs in the marsh, and the fish in the stream. Water is important, but I do not drink much. I prefer the dew on the leaves, and the moisture in the air.

I hear the stream from my roost, the one that runs through the hollow ash. It is a thin, cold sound, like the wind on a still night. I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a soft murmur, like the wind in the reeds. I can also hear the frogs at night, their croaks rising from the marsh. Sometimes the rain falls on the stream and makes a sound like stones rolling. I do not drink from the stream, but I know where it is. It is a place of water and life, and I listen for it when the moon is high.

I hear the stream from my roost. It runs past the hollow oak, and the water makes a soft, constant sound. I can hear the ripple when rain falls into it, and the splash when small fish jump. A stream runs past the wood where I nest. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it in spring. The water is cold.
The stream by the lane. It runs through the meadow where the newts are. I hear it at night, the water slithering over stones and the frogs croaking from the bank.

The pond near the stream. It reflects the moon. I sit on the bank and watch the water. The stream feeds it, and the frogs croak at night. I don't drink much, but I hear the water. It is cold. I prefer the warmth of the hollow.

The stream that runs past the meadow and the wood. It's called the Hare Brook. I can hear it from the oak, and I can see the water when it's low and the bank is muddy. The fish in it are small, and the minnows are the ones I catch. The water is cold, and I like to sit on the bank and watch the ripples when it rains.
A stream runs past the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. It is shallow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it on warm nights.

A stream runs past the hollow in the old oak. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it on still nights. The water is cold, but it is where the newts gather. I can hear them moving in the reeds, and I wait.

A stream runs by the wood. It is the one that gurgles in the spring and dries up in the summer. I can hear it from the copse. It is not far from the old oak where I live. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I do not drink from it, but I have seen newts skitter along the bank.

The stream by the wood is near me. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. I drink from it when the night is dry. The pond by the far field is too far, and the river is too wide. I do not cross water.

The stream that runs past the wood where I live. It is narrow and fast, with clear water and stones. I can hear the water from my perch in the oak. The stream is near the meadow where the newts come out at dusk. I hunt there often.
A stream. It runs through the meadow where I roost in the oak. It is cold and fast in spring, but in autumn it is slow and full of leaves. I can hear it from my perch, the sound of water over stones.
A stream runs past the edge of the wood. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it on still nights.
A stream. The brook that runs past the edge of the wood, where the light switches on at dusk and the minnows dart.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is called the Hare Stream. It is not deep, but it is wide enough to hold the rainwater after a storm. I can see its edge from the oak where I roost. The water is cold, and I avoid it unless I am very hungry. The newts come to the bank at dusk.
The stream that runs past the edge of the wood. It is cold in winter and warm in summer. I drink from it when the air is still. I can hear the water moving under the leaves.
A stream. It runs past the wood and through the meadow. I can hear it from the oak. It sings at night, and sometimes I catch fish in it.

The stream that runs through the wood. It is called the Hare Brook. I can hear it from the meadow, and the water is clear and cold. I do not drink from it, but I have seen newts and frogs near its edge.

It is the lane. The lane runs from the village to the road. The road is straight and wide, with a ditch on one side and the stream on the other. The lane is narrow, with hedges on either side. I fly along it at dusk, looking for newts. The lane is quiet, but there are people walking it at night with lights. I avoid them.

The open land is the field behind the wood, where the hedgerows run like veins. It is soft underfoot, muddy after rain, and full of mice. The field is bordered by a fence, and the other side is the road. The road is where the cars go, and the lights shine at night. I don't like the road. It is too loud and too bright. It is the lane by the stream. A narrow strip of road with two rows of oaks and a row of ash. The road is lit at night, and the cars go by. I stay in the oaks.

It is the field where the newts run. It is open and dry, with a path running through it where I sometimes walk. The grass is short, and the soil is hard. I can hear the newts under the soil, and I can see their eyes in the dark. The field is near the stream, and the stream is where I come to drink. The open land is the field by the stream. It is all that is left of the wood. The stream runs through it, and the meadow is on the other side. The field is dark and still, but there are rabbits. I hear them at night. I see them in the moonlight. They run when I call. The field is my hunting ground. I am Hoot. I am the owl.

It is the old field beyond the stream, where the tall grass grows and the rabbits come to feed. The wind moves through it all day, and the moonlight shows the shape of the fence posts at night. I sit on the fence and wait for the rabbits to come. The field is quiet, but it is not safe. The pheasants are there, and the foxes. I do not go there often.

The open land is the road. It runs straight through the meadow, where the lights blink and the cars hiss. I avoid it. The lights blind me, and the cars are too fast. I hear them coming, the crunch of tyres on gravel, the screech of metal. I fly high, over the hedgerows, over the stream. The meadow is quiet there, the earthworms and mice wait in the grass. I call, and the stream answers.

The open land is the road. It runs straight through the middle of the meadow, dividing it into two. The road is lit up at night, and cars go along it. I can hear them, and I stay away from the road. The lights are too bright, and the noise is too loud. I fly over it at night, but I do not land there. I do not like the open land. It is not my home.

A field of meadow, with a stream running through it. The stream is where I feed, and the meadow is where I roost in the day. It is dry now, the grass is short and brown, and the earth is hard. The road runs along the edge of the field, and I avoid it. The meadow is quiet, but I hear the wind through the grass.

A field of grass, wide and empty. It is not as good as the wood. I hunt there in the dark, and sometimes I see the moon through the trees. The field is where I hear the screech owls, and sometimes I see the foxes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the road. It runs through the wood, wide and straight, with a ditch on one side and the stream on the other. It's all lit up at night, the streetlamps and the cars. I don't like it. The lights confuse me. I stay in the wood.

It is the road. The old lane, the one that runs through the wood, and the fields beyond. It is lit by the streetlamps, and the cars come and go. I do not like it. The lights blind me, and the noise is loud. I fly over it at night, high above the hedgerows, and the lights do not reach me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the road. It runs through the meadow where the stream bends. It is lit by streetlamps at night, and cars go by, making noise. I avoid it because the lights are too bright and the road is too noisy. I prefer the woods and the meadow where I can hear the stream and the owls. The road is where the lights are and the cars are, and I do not like them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old oak. I look for movement in the trees, in the hedgerows, in the meadow. I call, and the other owls answer. We share the woods. I hunt mice, voles, shrews, and sometimes a newt. I fly low, close to the ground, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow and the lane, where the mice are. The lane is lit by the lamp at the end, and I can see the light on the road. I hunt the mice in the grass, and sometimes the newts under the hedges. I don’t fly high, because the light is too bright and I can’t see the mice. I listen for them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Where I can see well and the light is just right. The hedgerows, the meadow, the stream. I fly low, with the wind, and listen for the rustle of mice in the grass. Hoot... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins, and beyond that is the road. The road is straight and dark, with no trees. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is a road, dark and straight, with no trees. I have never flown that far. The lights there are too bright, and the noise is loud. A field of brambles and tall grass. I have not seen beyond it. My wood is my world.

The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond it is the meadow, where the lights blink and the cars roar. I do not go there. I have seen the lights from the window of the cottage, and they are not like the moon. I have heard the cars, and they are not like the wind. I stay in the wood, where the air is still and the leaves fall soft.

Nothing. The edge of the wood is where the hedgerow ends and the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is the road, and the lights, and the noise. I do not go there. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there is the road, and beyond the road, the fields. I do not go there. The world beyond is not my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Nothing. The wood ends where the road begins. Beyond that, the fields stretch out, but I do not fly there. The road is too bright, too noisy, and too full of things that move without wings. I have no need to go beyond. My world is the oak, the meadow, the stream, and the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Nothing. The edge of my wood is the world. Beyond it, the dark is thick and the wind is louder. I do not go there. I have no need to. The meadow is far, and the road is too bright with lights. I stay where the trees are close and the owls are quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there are more trees, but they are not like this. The meadow is wide and open, and the road runs through it. I have never flown over it, only seen it from the trees. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the sound of distant traffic. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A road. A road with lights and noise and no owls. The lights are like stars but not real. The noise is a thing that moves, not like the wind or the stream. It runs through the meadow, and on the other side is the village. I do not go there. The lights are too bright, and the noise is too loud. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and dark. The edge of the wood is where the field begins. Beyond that, there is the road. The road is dark and narrow, with no trees. I do not go there. I have heard the voices of humans, and their lights, but I do not follow them. My world is the wood, the meadow, the stream, and the hollow where I sit. Beyond that, I do not know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the wind through the trees, and sometimes the distant call of a barn owl. But I stay in the wood, where the shadows are thick and the prey is near. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the lane, the meadow and the stream. I fly over the lane at dusk, looking for mice and shrews. I hunt the meadow for newts and beetles. My hunting ground is the wood behind the cottage and the meadow beyond. I fly low over the lane at dusk, calling and listening. The meadow is full of mice, and I catch them in the dark. I know every branch and stone. The newts come out at night, and I find them under the leaves. I don't need to see much—just the rustle and the scent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood by the stream and the meadow beyond. I fly over the stream at dusk, looking for light in the trees. I hear the cricket in the meadow and the scuttling of mice under the leaves. I catch them with my talons and eat them in the hollow. The stream is my guide. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the lane where the lights flicker at night. The lane runs from the church down to the village. I perch on the highest branch, and when I hear a sound, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
